what_it_does: Graph neural networks (GNNs — AI models that learn from relationship data like social networks or molecular structures) are usually trained by repeatedly asking each node to collect features from its neighbors, which becomes explosively expensive as the graph grows. A newer family called pre-propagation GNNs (PP-GNNs) sidesteps this by doing all the neighbor-collection in a one-time preprocessing step, then training a standard dense model on the pre-collected features. This paper finds that PP-GNNs are theoretically efficient but in practice bottlenecked by data loading — pulling features from disk or host memory into the GPU — and proposes a set of system-level tricks that deliver up to 15× speedup over baseline PP-GNN implementations and up to two orders-of-magnitude speedup over sampling-based competitors on very large graphs.
method_in_detail:
The bottleneck. In standard GNN training, the expensive step is graph sampling (deciding which neighbors to include each mini-batch). PP-GNNs replace that with a one-time preprocessing that multiplies the input features by the graph's adjacency matrix several times to produce "hop features" (each node's feature blended with its 1-hop, 2-hop, ... k-hop neighbors). Training then uses only dense arithmetic — which should be fast on GPU. But profiling reveals that data loading consumes 88–91% of training time in unoptimized implementations, because the preprocessed features can be many times larger than the originals (5 hops × 1 operator = 6× the original size) and fetching thousands of scattered node rows from host memory is slow.

Fix 1: Efficient batch assembly. The baseline PyTorch data loader grabs one node's feature row at a time, launching a separate tiny operation per row. This wastes time on overhead. The fix uses PyTorch's index operator to copy all needed rows in a single call into a pinned memory buffer (pinned memory lets the GPU read it directly without an extra copy), then transfers that buffer to the GPU asynchronously. This alone gives 3.3× speedup.

Fix 2: Double-buffer prefetching. Even after fix 1, loading and computing still happen in sequence. Adding a second GPU buffer lets the data loader fill one buffer while the GPU computes on the other, hiding the load time behind computation. Together with fix 1, this adds another 1.9×.

Fix 3: Chunk reshuffling. Instead of randomly shuffling individual node indices each epoch (which produces random memory reads across a potentially terabyte-scale file), the method shuffles at the level of contiguous chunks of nodes. The GPU assembles batches from chunks, using its own much-higher-bandwidth memory. This replaces random host-memory reads with sequential chunk reads, adding another 2.4×. It also enables GPU Direct Storage (GDS), a technology that lets the GPU read chunks straight from an NVMe SSD without going through the CPU's memory at all — critical when the preprocessed data exceeds available host memory.

The result. The combination achieves 15× speedup over baseline PP-GNNs and up to 2 orders-of-magnitude higher training throughput than state-of-the-art sampling-based GNNs on graphs with 100 million nodes, while matching or exceeding their accuracy.
